cards.text: This is David son of Jesse, Israel's king, and the text calls these the last words of David. Last words, friend! Mine would probably be "Hold on... is the oven still on?"

cards.question: David starts by giving his titles. True or false: one of them is the one anointed by the God of Jacob.

cards.text: He keeps piling on titles. This is a man who sang whole songs to the LORD, like the one right before this (2 Samuel 22:1), so his last title fits him like a chef's hat.

cards.question: In his list of titles, David calls himself the sweet ___ of Israel.

cards.text: Now David tells you whose words these REALLY are. And the man is NOT taking the credit.

cards.question: According to David, who spoke through him in these last words?

cards.text: Then God speaks, and David calls Him the Rock of Israel. Right before this, David sang "The LORD is my rock" (2 Samuel 22:2), and I think he is NOT letting that name go.

cards.question: God tells David about a person who rules the people well. How does that ruler rule?

answers.text: With justice and in the fear of God
With a strong army and high walls
With great riches and many allies

cards.text: Then God paints a picture of that ruler, and it is GORGEOUS. I spent years in the back of a dark junk drawer, friend, so this one has me crying into my apron.

cards.question: What does God say a ruler who rules with justice is like?

answers.text: Like morning light at a cloudless dawn
Like a cedar standing tall in the forest
Like a wall around a strong city

cards.question: In God's picture of the good ruler, the light shines on dry grass that hasn't had any rain.

cards.text: Then David asks about his own house: "Is not my house right with God?" God had already made David a promise about that house (2 Samuel 7:16).

cards.question: True or false: David says the covenant God established with him is everlasting.
David says God's covenant with him is ordered and secured in every part. What does he ask about God next?

answers.text: Will He not bring about my full salvation
Will He not give me back my youth
Will He not make my enemies my servants

cards.text: Then the picture FLIPS, from sunrise and shiny grass to the worthless. Friend, I haven't had a mood swing like this since the day they slid me into that junk drawer.

cards.question: What does David say the worthless are all like?
David says the thorns in his picture are easy to gather up by hand.
David says the man who touches those thorns must be armed with ___ or with the shaft of a spear.
True or false: in David's picture, those thorns get carried far away before they are burned.

findings.problem: Card 1 calls David "Israel's king," but 2 Samuel 23:1 doesn't say that. It's a fact from outside the passage, and it has no reference.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This setup says David's last title fits a man who sang whole songs to the LORD. That points straight to "psalmist" for card 4 and rules out the other answers, "shepherd" and "warrior." The baker no longer reasons it out. The card gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "I think he is NOT letting that name go" links 2 Samuel 22:2 to 2 Samuel 23:3 as if David chose "Rock of Israel" because of his earlier song. Neither text says that. It adds a motive and makes a connection between passages that the texts don't state.

rule.text: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: The joke about years in a dark junk drawer making this picture moving hints that the picture is about light. That rules out the other answers on card 10, "cedar" and "wall," and gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "What does he ask about God next?" uses answers worded as the line itself ("Will He not bring about my full salvation"). The baker has to guess the next words of the poem instead of its meaning. A meaning question would work better, such as what David trusts God will bring about because the covenant is secure.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.
